Hanūmannāṭaka
------------------------------------------
The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि has inspired many a poet to compose literary works of great merit, based on the story as given there. The Hanūmannāṭaka—an ancient work attributed to हनुमान् himself—is one such. It is written in the style of a nāṭaka or a drama. Most of it is in poetry though containing some parts in prose also.
It has two recensions : the Mahā-nāṭaka edited by Madhusūdana-miśra of Bengal; the Hanūmannāṭaka edited by Dāmodaramiśra of western India.
The former contains 788 verses spread over 9 aṅkas (or scenes), whereas the latter has 578 verses in 14 aṅkas.
Dāmodaramiśra says that the king भोज got the text which had been inscribed on a piece of rock, through some fishermen.
The author is said to be the legendary हनुमान् himself.
Though it is called nāṭaka (drama) it does not have most of the normal, characteristic, features of Sanskrit dramas. It is more in line with the jātrā-literature of Bengal. (Jātrā is a drama in a rural setting in an open auditorium.)
The story begins with राम and लक्ष्मण accompanying the sage Viśvā-मित्र to his hermitage and practically follows the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि. The only change is रावण assuming the form of राम to tempt सीता, but failing in his attempt due to the warning of the ākāśavāṇī (voice from the void).
Some of the verses of this work are found in the well-known compositions of भवभूति (A. D. 800).

Hanumajjayantī
(‘birthday of हनुमान्’)
------------------------------------------
Whether Hanumān—also known as Māruti and Āñjaneya—was a historical personality or not, there is no doubt that he has created history by his exemplary life and behaviour. It is therefore but proper that he is remembered and honoured every year on his birthday, known as ‘Hanumaj-jayantī’.
According to Hindu mythological accounts, he was born as the son of Kesarī and Añjanādevī by the grace of शिव and वायु (the wind-god).
As regards the date, there are three different traditions assigning three different days for this event. They are: चैत्र Pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day during the lunar month of चैत्र, generally in March/April); Kārttika कृष्ण caturdaśī (the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the lunar month of Kārttika, generally in October/November); Mārgaśira śukla trayodaśī (thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the lunar month of Mārgaśira, generally in November/December).
The first and second dates are more popular in North India. The last is observed more in the South.
The observance of the vrata (religious vow) consists of ड़स्तिन्ग् during the day and worship of Śrī राम followed by the worship of हनुमान्, in the evening or night. Bathing the image of Hunumān with pañcāmṛta (a mixture of five sweet things viz., cow’s milk, curds, ghee, honey and sugar) is an important item of worship.
Applying scented oil to the image as also vermillion powder are essential.
The ड़ोओद् offering should include certain grams with jaggery.
Exhibition of wrestling talents by expert wrestlers before the image is an interesting aspect of the celebrations.
In some places, a garland of betal leaves or fried eatables is put on the image to ward off evils to oneself.
Ceremonial chanting of the Sundara-kāṇḍa (the fifth book of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa) is also a part of the rituals performed on this day.
